title: Understand what MP4 verification checks
description: Learn how Agent signatures, browser verification and careful key handling support evidence review.

chapters.title: A signature travels with the file

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Imagine a fictional team handing an original Agent recording to a reviewer. They want more than a reassuring filename. What does the verification feature add?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A suitably configured Agent signs a fingerprint when it finishes an MP4. That fingerprint describes selected structural properties of the recording, and the signature is embedded in the file. The corresponding public key lets a reviewer check it later.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So we don't need a separate little signature file that can get lost in an email?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Right. The signature travels inside the MP4. But the signing key must have been configured at capture time. A playable file isn't automatically a signed file.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Does checking our recording upload it to another analysis service?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The guide describes client-side verification. The page loads the file or a recording URL, reconstructs the fingerprint, extracts the embedded signature and checks it against the public key. The parsing and signature check happen in the browser.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can the reviewer check a copy stored outside Hub?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Yes, with the original signed file and the matching public key. Storage location isn't what makes the signature valid. Keep the original when moving evidence between systems.

chapters.title: Read the result within its boundary

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: If the result says valid, should we describe it as a universal guarantee about everything visible in the video?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. Describe the check accurately: the signature matches the reconstructed structural fingerprint and the key used for verification. The fingerprint isn't a hash of every decoded video sample, and verification isn't encryption or an independent investigation of the scene.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What if somebody helpfully trims and re-exports the file?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: That can change the signed structure and cause verification to fail. Request the original rather than treating an edited derivative as the original signed artifact. A failure can also involve a missing signature or a different key, so inspect the details.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should our team preserve alongside its evidence-handling process?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Protect the private signing key and retain the historical public keys needed to check older recordings. Someone with the private key is inside the trust boundary; the signature doesn't protect against that key being compromised.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Verify one original recording using the expected public key and record what the check establishes. Keep the original, key history and archive process straight. Use the linked guide for the exact metadata and operational configuration.

editorialStyle.tone: A short, high-level introduction for a first-time listener. Explain why the topic matters, build one mental model, and suggest one next action. Sound like two colleagues, not a narrated manual.
editorialStyle.scope: Aim for four to five minutes and roughly 500-550 spoken words. Use one fictional example and four short chapters. Leave identifiers, form limits, configuration, migration mechanics, and troubleshooting checklists in the linked guide. Keep essential caveats as practical consequences.
editorialStyle.humour: Optional: one or two brief, relevant light moments are enough. Prefer a relatable analogy over a separate joke. Never pad the overview with banter.
editorialStyle.reactions: Use occasional short, natural responses such as 'Oh, that makes sense' or 'Wait, so...' followed by a real question. Avoid repetitive praise, canned agreement, and filler.
editorialStyle.laughter: Optional: at most one or two light reactions such as 'Ha, fair point.' Never insert [laughs], SSML, or repeated ha-ha strings. These are spoken reactions, not a guarantee of genuine laughter from the current speech engine.
editorialStyle.intonation: Write real questions with question marks, use contractions, alternate short and longer sentences, and make contrasts explicit. Let punctuation and sentence rhythm suggest curiosity, surprise, and emphasis. Avoid all-caps shouting, excessive exclamation marks, and artificial pause tags.
editorialStyle.guardrails: Keep technical claims source-backed. Never mock the listener, joke about real victims, minimize security or data-loss risks, or let humour replace an explanation. Personality is optional; accuracy and clarity are not.
